strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: user-level private federated learning for large ASR models. Speaker-partitioned datasets and adaptation from LibriSpeech to Common Voice capture meaningful heterogeneity and domain shift.

The empirical investigation is extensive, covering three languages, seed-model quality, cohort sizes, data heterogeneity, optimizers, and augmentation. Transferring training settings from English to French and German provides useful evidence of robustness.

Per-layer clipping produces a substantial measured improvement at matched injected noise: Table 1 reports English test WER decreasing from 31.1% with global clipping to 20.4% with dimension-based clipping. The gradient diagnostics and targeted noise experiments provide useful insights into layer sensitivity.

The appendices document preprocessing, architecture, hyperparameters, and compute costs. Public datasets, explicit assumptions about non-private seed data, and candid discussion of extrapolation and secure aggregation provide valuable transparency. No serious ethical concern is apparent in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: The central convergence claim is not established. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1 − 8(1 − η_loc T_loc)^2 > 0, but its prescribed η_loc = Θ(1/(L sqrt(T_loc T))) makes κ approach −7 for fixed T_loc as T increases. Thus the stated asymptotic rate violates its own assumptions. Additional proof gaps include treating the adaptive preconditioner as independent of current DP noise in Equations 33–34, although it depends on the noisy update, and inferring bounded gradients from smoothness in Equation 20 without an appropriate domain or gradient-bound assumption.

The headline privacy–utility tradeoffs are projections, without validation at the claimed scale. The English experiments use 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024; the noise settings underlying the headline results have reported ε values around 10^7–10^8 at that scale. Obtaining ε = 4.5 or 7.2 requires extrapolating to approximately 7 million or 70 million users and cohorts of 204,800 while assuming comparable utility. Table 16 supports scaling without DP, but does not establish this assumption under noise. The disclosure is welcome; the evidence still falls short of demonstrating the advertised practical private training capability.

The claimed importance of combining LAMB with per-layer clipping is insufficiently isolated experimentally. Tables 8–9 compare optimizers without DP, whereas Section 3 asserts an advantage under DP. A controlled optimizer-by-clipping comparison at matched noise and tuning effort is needed to establish the interaction between these existing components. Evidence from one architecture also limits the broader claims about large models across domains.

The privacy accountant needs a clearer connection to the implemented mechanism. Theorem 1 assumes independent Poisson inclusion, while Algorithm 1, line 4, fixes cohort size. Appendix I.1 also asserts equivalence between client-side and server-side noise that requires qualification when cohort size is random. A matching accounting argument is necessary to substantiate the reported privacy guarantees.

Reproducibility remains limited by the code release being only planned and by the absence of reported uncertainty across repeated training runs. Exact configurations and accountant scripts would materially improve verification, while repeated-run results are particularly relevant to the small clipping improvements reported for French and German.
